¶
'''unbelievable''' (un-bẹ̄-lē′vạ-bl), ''a.'' Not to be believed; incredible. ''J. Udall.''
{{smaller block|The pine shot aloft from the crag to an ''unbelievable'' height.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Voyage of Maeldune.}}}}

'''unbelieved''' (un-bẹ̄-lēvd′), ''a.'' Not believed, credited, or trusted; also, incredible.
{{smaller block|<poem>As I, thus wrong’d, hence ''unbelieved'' go.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 119.}}
<poem>I made his valour stoop, and brought that name,
Soar’d to so ''unbeliev’d'' a height, to fall
Beneath mine.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unbeliever''' (un-bẹ̄-lē′vėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' An incredulous person; one who does not believe.—'''2.''' One who discredits Christian revelation, or the mission, character, and doctrines of Christ.
{{smaller block|They, having their conversation honest and holy amongst the ''unbelievers'', shined like virgin-tapers in the midst of an impure prison, and amused the eyes of the sons of darkness with the brightness of the flame.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 166.}}}}
'''3.''' One who does not believe in or hold any given religion.
{{smaller block|<poem>Who think through ''unbelievers''’ blood
Lies their directest path to heaven.</poem>
{{right|''Moore'', Fire-Worshippers.}}}}
='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Skeptic, Disbeliever'', etc. See ''infidel''.}}

'''unbelieving''' (un-bẹ̄-lē′ving), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not believing; incredulous; skeptical; doubting.—'''2.''' Infidel; discrediting divine revelation, or the mission, character, and doctrines of Christ: as, “the ''unbelieving'' Jews,” Acts xiv. 2.

'''unbelievingly''' (un-bẹ̄-lē′ving-li), ''adv.'' With unbelief. ''Clarke.''
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''unbellerophontic''' (un-be-ler-ō-fon′tik), ''a.'' Not like Bellerophon. See ''Bellerophon.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|In tones, looks, and manners he was embarrassing, and this I was willing to consider as the effect of my own ''unbellerophontic'' countenance and mien.
{{right|''Coleridge'', Letter to Sir George Beaumont.}}}}

'''unbeloved''' (un-bẹ̄-luvd′), ''a.'' Not loved. ''Dryden.''

'''unbelt''' (un-belt′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To ungird; remove the belt or girdle from.—'''2.''' To remove from the person by undoing the belt which supports it.
{{smaller block|The officers would have ''unbelted'' their swords.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Roman Meals.}}}}

'''unbend''' (un-bend′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''unbent'', ppr. ''unbending''. '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To become relaxed or unbent.—'''2.''' To rid one’s self of constraint; act with freedom; give up stiffness or austerity of manner; be affable.
{{smaller block|He [Charles II.] might be seen . . . striding among the trees, playing with his spaniels, and flinging corn to his ducks; and these exhibitions endeared him to the common people, who always love to see the great ''unbend.''
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., iv.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To free from flexure; make straight: as, to ''unbend'' a bow.
{{smaller block|''Unbending'' the rigid folds of the parchment cover, I found it to be a commission, under the hand and seal of Governor Shirley. ''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 33.
<poem>
I only meant
To draw up again the bow ''unbent.''
</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Mogg Megone.}}}}
'''2.''' To relax; remit from a strain or from exertion; set at ease for a time: as, to ''unbend'' the mind from study or care.
{{smaller block|<poem>
You do ''unbend'' your noble strength, to think
So brainsickly of things. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, ii. 2. 45.
</poem>}}

{{smaller block|The eternal, ''unbegotten'', and immutable God. {{right|''Stillingfleet.''}}}}

'''unbeknownst''' (un-bē-nōnst′), ''a.'' Same as ''unbeknown''. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|So by & by I creep up softly to my own old little room, not to disturb their pleasure, & ''unbeknownst'' to most.
{{right|''E. S. Phelps'', Sealed Orders.}}}}

'''unbelief''' (un-bē-lēf′), ''n.'' '''1.''' Incredulity; the withholding of belief; disbelief; especially, disbelief of divine revelation.
{{smaller block|<poem>[Truth] shines in all who do not shut it out
By dungeon doors of ''unbelief'' and doubt.</poem>
{{right|''Abraham Coles'', The Evangel, p. 181.}}}}
{{smaller block|Belief consists in accepting the affirmations of the soul; ''unbelief'', in denying them.
{{right|''Emerson'', Montaigne.}}}}
'''2.''' Disbelief of the truth of the gospel; distrust of God’s promises and faithfulness, etc. Mat. xiii. 58; Mark vi. 6; Heb. iii. 12.='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|Distrust.—'''1''' and '''2.''' ''Disbelief'', ''Unbelief'' (see ''disbelief''), skepticism.}}

{{smaller block|He that is ''unbeleveful'' to the sone, schal not se euerlastinge lyf.
{{right|''Wyclif'', John iii. 36.}}}}

{{smaller block|And anon the fadir of the child criynge with teeris seide: Lord, I beleve, help thou myn ''vnbilevefulness''. {{right|''Wyclif'', Mark ix. 24.}}}}

'''unbelievability''' (un-bē-lē-va-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' Incapability of being believed; incredibility.
{{smaller block|Boiling mud-oceans of Hypocrisy and ''Unbelievability.''
{{right|''Carlyle'', Life of Sterling, I. xv. (''Davies.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|They, having their conversation honest and holy amongst the ''unbelievers'', shined like virgin-tapers in the midst of an impure prison, and amused the eyes of the sons of darkness with the brightness of the flame.

'''unbellerophontic''' (un-be-ler-ō-fon′tik), ''a.'' Not like Bellerophon. See ''Bellerophon.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|In tones, looks, and manners he was embarrassing, and this I was willing to consider as the effect of my own ''unbellerophontic'' countenance and mien.

{{smaller block|He [Charles II.] might be seen . . . striding among the trees, playing with his spaniels, and flinging corn to his ducks; and these exhibitions endeared him to the common people, who always love to see the great ''unbend.''
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., iv.}}}}

</poem> She ''unbent'' her mind afterwards, over a book.
{{right|''Lamb'', Mrs. Battle on Whist.}}}}
'''3.''' ''Naut.'': (''a'') To unfasten from the yards and stays, as sails. (''b'') To cast loose, as a cable from the anchor. (''c'') To untie, as a rope.

'''unbended†''' (un-ben′ded), ''a.'' Relaxed; unbent.
{{smaller block|<poem>He ruddy Nectar pours,
And Jove regales in his ''unbended'' Hours.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', Hymn to Venus.}}}}

'''unbending<sup>1</sup>''' (un-ben′ding), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''bending''.] '''1.''' Not suffering flexure; not bending.
{{smaller block|Flies o’er the ''unbending'' corn and skims along the main.
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 373.}}}}
'''2.''' Unyielding; inflexible; firm.
{{smaller block|Nobody demands from a party the ''unbending'' equity of a judge.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Warren Hastings.}}
The arrogant Strafford and the ''unbending'' Laud had as bitter rivals in the palace as they had enemies in the nation.
{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. U. S., I. 379.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Unbending column''', a column in which, as in a Doric column, the thickness in proportion to the length is so great that fracture under vertical pressure can occur only by detrusion, or by sliding apart in a plane or planes whose angle is dependent upon the material, and not by tendency to lateral bending inducing transverse fracture.}}

'''unbending<sup>2</sup>''' (un-ben′ding), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''unbend'', ''v.''] A relaxing; remission from a strain; temporary ease.
{{smaller block|Stalwart and rubicund men they were, second only, if second, to S., champion of the county, and not incapable of genial ''unbendings'' when the fasces were laid aside.
{{right|''Lowell'', Fireside Travels, p. 35.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
